title: Setup and Deployment
text:
Install Quarto >= 1.4 from https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/
Verify:
quarto --version



Create and activate a dedicated environment (conda or venv):
# Option A: conda
conda create -n quartosite python=3.11
conda activate quartosite

# Option B: venv
python -m venv .venv
# Windows
.venv\Scripts\activate
# macOS / Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
Install dependencies:
pip install numpy pandas scikit-learn plotly umap-learn torch torchvision
Or use the provided requirements file:
pip install -r requirements.txt



numpy>=1.24
pandas>=2.0
scikit-learn>=1.3
plotly>=5.17
umap-learn>=0.5
torch>=2.0
torchvision>=0.15





cd /path/to/QuartoSite
quarto preview
This starts a live-reload server at http://localhost:22222.
The first render will execute all Python chunks and cache results under _freeze/. Subsequent renders skip re-execution unless source files change (controlled by execute: freeze: auto in _quarto.yml).




quarto render
Output is written to docs/. Open docs/index.html in a browser to inspect the result before publishing.






Ensure the repository has GitHub Pages configured to serve from the docs/ folder on the main branch, or use the gh-pages branch method:
# Method A: docs/ folder on main (simpler)
# In GitHub → Settings → Pages → Source: Deploy from branch → main / docs
quarto render
git add docs/
git commit -m "build: render site"
git push

# Method B: Quarto managed gh-pages branch (recommended)
quarto publish gh-pages
For Method B, the first run will prompt for confirmation and create the gh-pages branch automatically.



quarto publish gh-pages
Quarto renders, then pushes to the gh-pages branch. The site is live at https://<your-github-username>.github.io/<repo-name>/.





If you add a references.bib file and want APA formatting, download the CSL:
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/citation-style-language/styles/master/apa.csl
Then add to _quarto.yml:
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl





Replace G-XXXXXXXXXX in _quarto.yml with real GA4 Measurement ID, or remove the key
Replace 0000-0000-0000-0000 ORCID in index.qmd and contact.qmd
Replace all DOI: PLACEHOLDER entries in publications.qmd
Review and correct research descriptions in research.qmd
Update CV sections in cv.qmd (or ensure cv/cv.pdf is current)
Update project descriptions in projects/
Review ASSUMPTIONS.md and confirm all inferences are correct

title: Projects
text: An overview of current and recent research projects. Each project page contains a description of the scientific question, methods, collaborators, and outputs.

title: Projects
text:
Species Distribution Modelling with DeepMaxEnt

Neural network-based extension of the MaxEnt framework for multi-species distribution modelling. The model learns non-linear environmental feature interactions while preserving the maximum entropy principle as a regularisation constraint, producing calibrated suitability maps for presence-only data.
Project page → | Code | DOI: 10.1111/2041-210x.70262

title: Projects
section: Smart Viticulture and IoT Sensor Fusion
text:
Smart Viticulture and IoT Sensor Fusion

Integration of IoT sensor networks (microclimate, soil moisture, canopy imaging) with near-infrared spectral data for real-time monitoring of grapevine stress and disease onset. Machine learning models fuse asynchronous, heterogeneous streams to provide decision support for precision viticulture.
Collaborators: UMR AGAP, INRAE Status: In progress

title: Projects
section: Genomic Selection and Phenotyping for Perennial Crops
text:
Genomic Selection and Phenotyping for Perennial Crops

Multi-task learning models for genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) prediction in perennial species (grapevine, tropical trees, maize). Non-destructive spectral phenotyping with NIR is integrated alongside genomic markers to reduce the cost per selection cycle and to characterise genotype-by-environment interactions.
Team: GSP — CIRAD / UMR AGAP Status: In progress

title: Maxime Ryckewaert
text:
Research Themes
Representation learning from complex biological signals. Spectral, temporal, and genomic data share a structural challenge: informative variation is entangled with noise, domain shifts, and missing modalities. My research develops transformer-based architectures and multivariate methods that learn compact, transferable representations, with explicit uncertainty quantification and interpretability constraints.
Multivariate and multi-modal methods for perennial crop genetics and phenotyping. For perennial crops in tropical and Mediterranean environments, including tropical trees, grapevine, and other long-cycle species, I develop statistical and machine learning methods integrating genomic, spectral, and time-series data. Research directions include multi-task learning, data fusion across modalities, genomic selection, and the characterisation of genotype-by-environment interactions, with an emphasis on model interpretability.
Species distribution modelling and ecological inference. I develop probabilistic and machine learning frameworks to model species distributions from environmental and occurrence data, including for wild plant species. This work focuses on integrating heterogeneous spatial predictors, learning ecologically meaningful latent structures, and producing interpretable outputs to support biodiversity monitoring and ecological forecasting under environmental change.

title: Maxime Ryckewaert
text:
Recent Highlights



Irokube — Critical habitat mapping enhanced by data cubes
The project Irokube explores the use of biodiversity data cubes combined with satellite and bioclimatic data cubes to identify critical habitats using Deep-SDM and habitat distribution models (HDM). A case study in Belgium illustrated the approach at the B-Cubed Hackathon 2024. Hackathon report





Talk at World Biodiversity Forum 2024, Davos
Presentation on Disentangling Observation Biases for Species Distribution Modeling, addressing sampling biases in presence-only citizen science data. We developed a simulation framework to evaluate point process loss functions in mitigating these biases for deep learning-based SDMs.





Best Poster Award — IASIM 2022
One of three Best Poster Awards at the International Conference on Spectral Imaging (IASIM 2022) for work on predicting stomatal conductance and transpiration in grapevine from hyperspectral imaging combined with climate data. Conference award

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
This notebook introduces the chemometrics dataset used throughout this course: near-infrared spectral measurements from hyperspectral imaging of grape berries, paired with sugar content measurements (g/L). We will explore the dataset structure, visualise the raw spectra, and examine the distribution of the target variable.



Ryckewaert, M. et al. (2023). Dataset containing spectral data from hyperspectral imaging and sugar content measurements of grape berries in various maturity stages. Data in Brief. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dib.2022.108822


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.colors as pc
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

NAVY  = '#1b3a5c'
TEAL  = '#2a7f7f'
GREEN = '#78BE20'
GRAY  = '#868e96'
COLORS_VAR = {'SYRAH': NAVY, 'MAUZAC': TEAL, 'FER': GREEN}

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
This notebook introduces the chemometrics dataset used throughout this course: near-infrared spectral measurements from hyperspectral imaging of grape berries, paired with sugar content measurements (g/L). We will explore the dataset structure, visualise the raw spectra, and examine the distribution of the target variable.



Ryckewaert, M. et al. (2023). Dataset containing spectral data from hyperspectral imaging and sugar content measurements of grape berries in various maturity stages. Data in Brief. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dib.2022.108822


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.colors as pc
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

NAVY  = '#1b3a5c'
TEAL  = '#2a7f7f'
GREEN = '#78BE20'
GRAY  = '#868e96'
COLORS_VAR = {'SYRAH': NAVY, 'MAUZAC': TEAL, 'FER': GREEN}

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
Loading the dataset
The CSV file uses a semicolon delimiter and the first column is a row index. The Variety column identifies the grape cultivar; Sugar content (g/l) is our response variable; the remaining 204 columns are spectral reflectance values at wavelengths from approximately 397 nm to 1004 nm (visible to near-infrared range).

df = pd.read_csv('data/chemometrics/DATASET.csv', sep=';', index_col=0)

print(f"Dataset shape: {df.shape}  ({df.shape[0]} samples, {df.shape[1]} columns)")
print(f"Missing values: {df.isnull().sum().sum()}")
df.head(3)

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
section: Separating metadata, target, and spectral matrix
text:
Separating metadata, target, and spectral matrix
We split the dataframe into three parts: - variety: grape cultivar label (SYRAH, MAUZAC, FER) - y: sugar content in g/L (response variable) - X: spectral reflectance matrix, shape (274, 204) - wavelengths: wavelength axis in nm, extracted from column names (x.397.32 → 397.32)

variety = df['Variety']
y = df['Sugar content (g/l)']

spectral_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith('x.')]
X = df[spectral_cols].values
wavelengths = np.array([float(c.replace('x.', '', 1)) for c in spectral_cols])

print(f"Samples:          {X.shape[0]}")
print(f"Spectral bands:   {X.shape[1]}")
print(f"Wavelength range: {wavelengths[0]:.1f} – {wavelengths[-1]:.1f} nm")
print(f"Varieties:        {variety.value_counts().to_dict()}")

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
section: Raw spectra — coloured by sugar content
text:
Raw spectra — coloured by sugar content
Each line represents one berry sample. A representative subset of 80 samples is coloured by sugar content (blue = low, red = high) to reveal any spectral gradient correlated with the response. The characteristic features of grape berry VIS–NIR spectra include:

A sharp drop in reflectance below ~700 nm due to chlorophyll and anthocyanin absorption
A progressive increase from ~700 nm toward the NIR plateau
A water absorption dip around 970 nm reducing reflectance at the right edge


# Representative subset (80 evenly-spaced samples) for visualisation
n_show = 80
show_idx = np.linspace(0, len(X) - 1, n_show, dtype=int)
y_show = y.values[show_idx]
y_norm_show = (y_show - y_show.min()) / (y_show.max() - y_show.min())
trace_colors = pc.sample_colorscale('RdYlBu_r', y_norm_show.tolist())

fig = go.Figure()

for i, (idx_i, color, sugar) in enumerate(zip(show_idx, trace_colors, y_show)):
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=wavelengths, y=X[idx_i],
        mode='lines',
        line=dict(color=color, width=0.8),
        opacity=0.5,
        showlegend=False,
        hovertemplate=f'Sugar: {sugar:.1f} g/L<extra></extra>'
    ))

# Invisible trace to generate the colour bar
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=[None], y=[None], mode='markers',
    marker=dict(
        colorscale='RdYlBu_r',
        color=[float(y.min()), float(y.max())],
        cmin=float(y.min()), cmax=float(y.max()),
        colorbar=dict(title='Sugar content (g/L)', thickness=15, len=0.9),
        showscale=True, size=1
    ),
    showlegend=False
))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Wavelength (nm)',
    yaxis_title='Reflectance',
    title=f'VIS–NIR spectra coloured by sugar content ({n_show} representative samples)',
    template='simple_white',
    height=430
)
fig.show()

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
Spectra by variety
Plotting individual spectra and the mean per variety helps identify systematic differences in reflectance level or spectral shape between SYRAH, MAUZAC, and FER — inter-variety variability that a calibration model must handle.

fig = go.Figure()

for var, color in COLORS_VAR.items():
    mask = (variety == var).values
    X_var = X[mask]
    n_var = mask.sum()

    # Individual spectra (faint — skip legend to avoid clutter)
    for spectrum in X_var:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=wavelengths, y=spectrum,
            mode='lines',
            line=dict(color=color, width=0.5),
            opacity=0.15,
            showlegend=False,
            hoverinfo='skip'
        ))

    # Mean spectrum (bold, with legend entry)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=wavelengths, y=X_var.mean(axis=0),
        mode='lines',
        line=dict(color=color, width=2.5),
        name=f'{var} mean (n={n_var})'
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Wavelength (nm)',
    yaxis_title='Reflectance',
    title='Raw spectra by variety — individual traces and mean',
    template='simple_white',
    height=430,
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.02, xanchor='right', x=1)
)
fig.show()

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
Distribution of sugar content
Sugar content (g/L) is the calibration target. Visualising its distribution allows us to assess range coverage, potential skewness or multimodality (e.g., driven by variety), and whether a stratified train/test split will be necessary.

fig = make_subplots(
    rows=1, cols=2,
    subplot_titles=['Distribution by variety', 'Overall kernel density estimate']
)

# Left panel: overlaid histograms per variety
for var, color in COLORS_VAR.items():
    mask = variety == var
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Histogram(
            x=y[mask].values, nbinsx=15,
            name=var, opacity=0.65,
            marker_color=color
        ),
        row=1, col=1
    )

# Right panel: KDE
y_range = np.linspace(float(y.min()) - 15, float(y.max()) + 15, 300)
kde_vals = gaussian_kde(y)(y_range)

fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=y_range, y=kde_vals,
        mode='lines', fill='tozeroy',
        fillcolor='rgba(27,58,92,0.2)',
        line=dict(color=NAVY, width=2),
        name='KDE', showlegend=False
    ),
    row=1, col=2
)

# Vertical lines for mean and median
for xval, color, label, dash in [
    (float(y.mean()),   TEAL,  f'Mean = {y.mean():.1f} g/L',   'dash'),
    (float(y.median()), GREEN, f'Median = {y.median():.1f} g/L', 'dot')
]:
    kde_at_x = float(gaussian_kde(y)(xval))
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[xval, xval], y=[0, kde_at_x * 1.1],
            mode='lines',
            line=dict(color=color, dash=dash, width=1.8),
            name=label, showlegend=True
        ),
        row=1, col=2
    )

fig.update_xaxes(title_text='Sugar content (g/L)')
fig.update_yaxes(title_text='Count', row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text='Density', row=1, col=2)
fig.update_layout(
    barmode='overlay',
    template='simple_white',
    height=380,
    legend=dict(orientation='h', yanchor='bottom', y=1.05)
)
fig.show()

title: Part 1 — Spectral Data Exploration
text:
Descriptive statistics

print("=== Sugar content (g/L) — overall ===")
print(y.describe().round(2))
print()
print("=== Per-variety breakdown ===")
print(df.groupby('Variety')['Sugar content (g/l)'].describe().round(2))
print()
print("=== Spectral matrix ===")

title: Species Distribution Modelling with DeepMaxEnt
text:
Predicting where species occur — and how distributions will shift under climate change — is a central challenge in conservation biology and ecology. Classical MaxEnt models this from presence-only occurrence data by selecting the maximum entropy distribution consistent with observed environmental feature expectations. This project extends the MaxEnt framework to neural networks, allowing non-linear feature interactions while preserving the theoretical guarantees of entropy regularisation.
Publication: Ryckewaert M. et al. (2026). Applying the maximum entropy principle to neural networks enhances multi-species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. DOI: 10.1111/2041-210x.70262

title: Species Distribution Modelling with DeepMaxEnt
text:
Scientific question
Can embedding the maximum entropy principle as a neural network loss function improve the calibration and transferability of multi-species distribution models compared to classical MaxEnt and binary cross-entropy-trained networks, particularly in regions with sparse occurrence records?

title: Species Distribution Modelling with DeepMaxEnt
text:
Approach

From MaxEnt to neural networks
Classical MaxEnt finds the distribution \(\hat{p}\) that maximises entropy subject to matching observed feature expectations at occurrence locations:
\[\hat{p} = \arg\max_p H(p) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbb{E}_p[f_k] = \mathbb{E}_\text{occ}[f_k]\]
The solution is a Gibbs distribution with linear feature weights. DeepMaxEnt replaces the linear feature map with a neural network \(g_\theta\), trained by minimising the equivalent Poisson process negative log-likelihood:
\[\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{x \in \mathcal{P}} g_\theta(x) + \log \frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} e^{g_\theta(x)}\]
where \(\mathcal{P}\) are presence sites and \(\mathcal{B}\) are background points approximating the available environmental space.


Multi-species architecture
A shared neural backbone extracts transferable environmental representations across all modelled species. Species-specific linear heads map the shared embedding to per-species log-suitability scores. This joint training improves performance for rare species by borrowing statistical strength from co-occurring species with denser occurrence records.


Environmental predictors
Models are trained on CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ global climate layers (Brun et al., 2022) at kilometre resolution, and can incorporate additional remote sensing layers (NDVI time series, canopy height, land cover). Standardisation is performed using background point statistics to ensure ecologically meaningful scaling.

title: Research
text: My research develops machine learning and statistical methods for biological systems that produce high-dimensional, heterogeneous data — from DNA sequences and spectral measurements to satellite imagery and occurrence records. A unifying thread across application domains is the multi-scale structure of biological variation: from the genome, through the individual organ (leaf, root, fruit), to the canopy and the landscape. Exploiting that structure requires methods that can fuse information across scales and modalities while remaining interpretable to biologists and breeders.

title: Research
text:
Motivation
Two converging pressures define the context of this work.
The data abundance problem. High-throughput phenotyping platforms, genomic arrays, and remote sensing now generate data at scales that exceed classical statistical workflows. A single UAV flight over a trial produces gigabytes of hyperspectral imagery; a genotyping array characterises hundreds of thousands of loci per individual. The bottleneck has shifted from data collection to extraction of reliable biological signal from these streams.
The environmental urgency. Perennial crops — grapevine, tropical trees, and others with multi-decade production cycles — face mounting pressure from climate change. Breeding cycles for these species span 10–20 years, making early, accurate prediction of genotype performance under future environments a critical bottleneck for food security and agroecosystem sustainability. Similarly, biodiversity monitoring requires scalable, automated tools to track species distribution shifts across large spatial extents and over time.
Standard machine learning approaches — developed for clean, balanced, large-scale benchmarks — transfer poorly to these contexts, which are characterised by small annotated datasets, heterogeneous measurement conditions, missing modalities, and strong domain-shift between training and deployment environments.

title: Research
text:
Open Questions

Multi-modal fusion across biological scales
Biological phenotypes emerge from the interplay of genetic, physiological, and environmental processes operating at different spatial and temporal scales. No single sensor captures all relevant variation. The central methodological question is: how can information from complementary modalities — genomic markers, spectral reflectance, morphological measurements, climatic time series — be fused in a principled way when modalities are partially observed and measured on different subsets of individuals?
Existing approaches (early fusion, late fusion, kernel methods) make strong assumptions about data alignment that rarely hold in field experiments. Architectures that handle missing modalities and learn cross-modal correspondences in a self-supervised regime are an open research direction.


Interpretability under biological constraints
Black-box predictions are not sufficient for plant breeding or ecological management: decisions must be justified to stakeholders and grounded in biological knowledge. What architectural and training choices make deep models interpretable without sacrificing predictive performance? Specific questions include the identifiability of latent representations, the faithfulness of attribution methods (SHAP, integrated gradients) on tabular and spectral data, and the design of models that encode domain-specific invariances (e.g. spectral wavelength ordering, phylogenetic structure).


New AI methods for ecological inference
Species distribution models must extrapolate beyond observed conditions — to novel climates, unstudied regions, or future time horizons. How can neural network-based SDMs produce calibrated uncertainty estimates that reflect genuine extrapolation risk, rather than interpolation confidence? Work building on the maximum entropy principle (MaxEnt) applied to neural architectures offers a tractable route: by constraining the learned distribution to maximum entropy subject to feature constraints, the model defaults to conservatism in data-sparse regions rather than overconfident extrapolation.

title: Research
text:
Approach

From genome to leaf to canopy
The multi-scale structure of plant phenotypes motivates a hierarchical research programme:








Scale
Data types
Key questions




Genome
SNP arrays, sequence variants
Genomic selection, G×E interaction, polygenic architecture


Organ
VIS–NIR/SWIR spectra, biochemical assays
Non-destructive trait prediction, stress detection, quality monitoring


Plant / plot
RGB and multispectral imagery, 3D point clouds
Architectural traits, growth dynamics, phenological stages


Landscape
Satellite time series, climate layers, occurrence records
Species distribution, habitat connectivity, ecological forecasting



Each scale requires specific methods, but the research program seeks bridges: transfer learning from high-data scales to low-data scales, and fusion architectures that integrate information across levels.


Near-infrared and VIS–NIR spectroscopy
Reflectance spectroscopy provides a rapid, non-destructive window onto leaf and fruit biochemistry. I develop regression models — from partial least squares to convolutional regressors — that predict agronomic traits (water content, sugar concentration, chlorophyll) from spectral profiles, with explicit handling of inter-instrument variability and domain shift between calibration and application conditions. Applications include water stress detection in grapevine and quality monitoring during berry maturation (Ryckewaert et al., 2022; Courand et al., 2022).


Genomic selection and genotype-by-environment modelling
In perennial crops, the long juvenile phase makes early marker-assisted selection particularly valuable. I develop multi-task learning and mixed-model frameworks for genomic estimated breeding value (GEBV) prediction that explicitly model G×E interactions and share statistical strength across related environments. Integrating spectral phenotyping with genomic data via multi-block and multi-modal fusion is an active direction.


Neural networks for species distribution modelling
Classical MaxEnt constrains the predicted distribution to maximum entropy while matching empirical feature expectations — a statistically principled form of regularisation for presence-only data. Embedding this principle in neural architectures allows the model to learn non-linear feature interactions while retaining the theoretical guarantees of MaxEnt against overfitting in data-sparse regions (Ryckewaert et al., 2026). Current extensions address multi-species joint modelling and the incorporation of remote sensing predictors.


Transformer and attention-based architectures
Self-attention mechanisms are naturally suited to spectral and genomic sequences, where local and long-range dependencies coexist. I investigate the application of transformer architectures to 1D spectral regression and to multi-omics integration, with particular attention to attention head interpretability as a route to wavelength-level feature attribution.

title: Research
text:
Impact
Crop improvement for perennial species. Accelerating breeding cycles through accurate early prediction of performance reduces the time-to-market for new varieties adapted to drought, disease, or changing phenological windows — directly relevant to CIRAD’s mandate for sustainable tropical and Mediterranean agriculture.
Biodiversity monitoring at scale. Calibrated, spatially explicit species distribution maps with uncertainty estimates support habitat management, protected area planning, and reporting under international biodiversity frameworks (CBD, IPBES).
Methodological contributions. Each application problem motivates general methodological questions — about multi-modal fusion, interpretability, and distribution shift — whose solutions are publishable and transferable across biological domains.

text:
Learning objectives
After completing this module you should be able to:

title: Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling
text:
Background: why MaxEnt for SDMs?

The presence-only problem
Field surveys rarely confirm absences. A species not recorded at a location may be absent, or it may simply not have been detected. Species distribution models (SDMs) are therefore typically trained on presence-only data: a set of confirmed occurrence locations \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\} \subset \mathcal{X}\), where \(\mathcal{X}\) is the environmental space of the study region.
The challenge is to infer a probability distribution \(\hat{p}(x)\) — the predicted occurrence probability — from presences alone, without a confirmed absence class.


The MaxEnt principle
The classical solution (Phillips et al., 2006) applies the maximum entropy principle: among all distributions consistent with the observed data, choose the one with maximum entropy — i.e. the least informative one given the evidence. Formally, MaxEnt finds \(\hat{p}\) that solves:
\[\hat{p} = \arg\max_{p} H(p) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}_{p}[f_k(x)] = \mathbb{E}_{\text{occ}}[f_k(x)], \quad k = 1, \ldots, K\]
where \(H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x)\) is entropy, \(f_k\) are feature functions of the environment (temperature, precipitation, …), and the constraints enforce that the model’s expected feature values match those observed at occurrence locations.
The solution takes a Gibbs distribution form:
\[\hat{p}(x) \propto \exp\!\left(\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x)\right)\]
where \(\lambda_k\) are Lagrange multipliers, equivalent to the weights of a log-linear model.


From linear features to neural networks
Classical MaxEnt is restricted to hand-crafted, fixed feature functions (linear, quadratic, product terms). DeepMaxEnt replaces this fixed feature map with a shared neural network \(g_\theta : \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^C\), which learns a common latent environmental representation across all modelled species jointly. The occurrence intensity of species \(j\) at site \(i\) is obtained by combining the shared network output with species-specific parameters \(\alpha_j\):
\[\lambda_{ij} = \exp\!\left(\alpha_j^\top\, g_\theta(x_i)\right)\]
The DeepMaxEnt loss is defined as a weighted sum of species-wise cross-entropy losses, with intensities normalised across all \(K\) sites for each species independently:
\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \mathbf{Y}) = -\frac{1}{KN} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} y_{ij} \log\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{kj}}\right)\]
where \(y_{ij}\) is the observed presence of species \(j\) at site \(i\), \(\lambda_{ij}\) the predicted intensity, \(K\) the number of sites (background + presence), and \(N\) the number of species. Equivalently, at the parameter level:
\[\mathcal{L}(\theta, \alpha) = -\sum_j \left[ \frac{1}{n_j} \sum_{i \in \text{occ}_j} \log \lambda_{ij} - \log \sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} \lambda_{jx} \right]\]
This per-species normalisation decouples parameter updates from absolute occurrence counts, distinguishing DeepMaxEnt from a standard Poisson loss in the multi-species setting: a species with 5 occurrences and one with 500 contribute equally to the gradient, preventing high-frequency species from dominating training.

title: Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling
text:
Step 4 — Load pre-cropped environmental rasters
The CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ rasters are already cropped to the study region extent. Each .tif file contains one bioclimatic variable at ~1 km resolution.

raster_dir = 'data/deepmaxent/cropped_rasters/'
raster_files = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(raster_dir) if f.endswith('.tif')])

env_bands = []
transform_ref, crs_ref = None, None
lon_min = lon_max = lat_min = lat_max = None

for fname in tqdm(raster_files, desc='Loading rasters'):
    with rasterio.open(os.path.join(raster_dir, fname)) as src:
        band = src.read(1).astype(float)
        if src.nodata is not None:
            band[band == src.nodata] = np.nan
        env_bands.append(band)
        if transform_ref is None:
            transform_ref = src.transform
            crs_ref       = src.crs
            lon_min, lat_min, lon_max, lat_max = src.bounds

env_stack = np.stack(env_bands, axis=0)   # (n_vars, height, width)
print(f"Environmental stack: {env_stack.shape}  "
      f"({env_stack.shape[0]} variables, {env_stack.shape[1]}×{env_stack.shape[2]} pixels)")
print(f"Extent: lon [{lon_min:.3f}, {lon_max:.3f}]  lat [{lat_min:.3f}, {lat_max:.3f}]")

Environmental stack: (19, 378, 418)  (19 variables, 378×418 pixels)
Extent: lon [-86.017, -82.534]  lat [8.139, 11.289]

title: Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling
text:
Step 5 — Prepare training tensors
The model requires two sets of points:

Presence points — the rasterised occurrence coordinates (one record per pixel).
Background points — randomly sampled pixels from the study region, representing the available environmental space. These approximate the partition function in the MaxEnt loss.


n_vars, height, width = env_stack.shape

# Rasterise occurrences vectorised (rowcol accepts arrays)
rows, cols = rasterio.transform.rowcol(
    transform_ref,
    df_plants['decimalLongitude'].values,
    df_plants['decimalLatitude'].values
)
rows, cols = np.asarray(rows), np.asarray(cols)
valid_occ  = (rows >= 0) & (rows < height) & (cols >= 0) & (cols < width)

presence_grid = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=int)
np.add.at(presence_grid, (rows[valid_occ], cols[valid_occ]), 1)

pres_rows, pres_cols = np.where(presence_grid > 0)
X_pres = env_stack[:, pres_rows, pres_cols].T   # (n_pres, n_vars)

# Background: random sample of non-NaN pixels
valid_mask = ~np.any(np.isnan(env_stack), axis=0)
valid_rows, valid_cols = np.where(valid_mask)
n_bg   = min(10_000, len(valid_rows))
bg_idx = np.random.choice(len(valid_rows), n_bg, replace=False)
X_bg   = env_stack[:, valid_rows[bg_idx], valid_cols[bg_idx]].T  # (n_bg, n_vars)

# Standardise on background statistics
scaler   = StandardScaler().fit(X_bg)
X_pres_s = scaler.transform(X_pres)
X_bg_s   = scaler.transform(X_bg)

X_pres_t = torch.tensor(X_pres_s, dtype=torch.float32)
X_bg_t   = torch.tensor(X_bg_s,   dtype=torch.float32)

print(f"Presence pixels: {X_pres_t.shape[0]}  |  Background pixels: {X_bg_t.shape[0]}")
print(f"Environmental variables: {X_pres_t.shape[1]}")

Presence pixels: 859  |  Background pixels: 10000
Environmental variables: 19


Why standardise on background statistics? Background points represent the marginal distribution of environmental conditions in the study region — the reference against which presences are evaluated. Using background statistics for standardisation ensures the scaling is environmentally meaningful rather than biased towards conditions where the species occurs.

title: Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling
section: Step 6 — Build and train the DeepMaxEnt model
text:
Step 6 — Build and train the DeepMaxEnt model
The DeepMaxEnt architecture consists of a shared neural network backbone \(g_\theta : \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^C\) followed by \(N\) species-specific linear heads \(\alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}^C\). The predicted intensity of species \(j\) at site \(i\) is \(\lambda_{ij} = \exp(\alpha_j^\top g_\theta(x_i))\).
Training minimises the species-wise normalised cross-entropy:
\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \mathbf{Y}) = -\frac{1}{KN} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} y_{ij} \log\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{kj}}\right)\]
Normalising across sites for each species independently ensures that rare and common species contribute equally to gradient updates.

# Concatenate presence and background — the loss needs all sites at once
all_X = torch.cat([X_pres_t, X_bg_t], dim=0)    # (n_pres + n_bg, n_vars)
all_y = torch.zeros(len(all_X), 1)               # presence labels: 0 = background
all_y[:len(X_pres_t)] = 1.0                      # 1 = presence

n_features = X_pres_t.shape[1]
model     = deepmaxent_model(input_size=n_features, hidden_size=128, output_size=1, hidden_nbr=3)
criterion = deepmaxent_loss()

optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=50, gamma=0.5)

n_epochs = 150
losses = []

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(all_X), all_y)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    scheduler.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())
    if (epoch + 1) % 30 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:3d}/{n_epochs}  loss = {loss.item():.4f}")

Epoch  30/150  loss = 0.6626
Epoch  60/150  loss = 0.6508
Epoch  90/150  loss = 0.6454
Epoch 120/150  loss = 0.6418
Epoch 150/150  loss = 0.6389



fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=list(range(1, len(losses) + 1)), y=losses,
    mode='lines', line=dict(color=NAVY, width=2), name='Training loss'
))
for ep, label in [(50, 'LR ×0.5'), (100, 'LR ×0.5')]:
    fig.add_vline(x=ep, line_dash='dash', line_color=TEAL, line_width=1.4,
                  annotation_text=label, annotation_position='top right',
                  annotation_font_size=11)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Epoch', yaxis_title='DeepMaxEnt loss',
    title='Training convergence — DeepMaxEnt',
    template='simple_white', height=340

Step 7 — Predict and map habitat suitability

# Predict on all valid pixels
valid_env = env_stack[:, valid_rows, valid_cols].T
X_full_s  = scaler.transform(valid_env)
X_full_t  = torch.tensor(X_full_s, dtype=torch.float32)

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    logit_scores = model(X_full_t).numpy().flatten()

# Convert log-suitability to [0, 1] via logistic transform
suitability = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit_scores))

suit_grid = np.full((height, width), np.nan)
suit_grid[valid_rows, valid_cols] = suitability

print(f"Suitability range: {np.nanmin(suitability):.3f} – {np.nanmax(suitability):.3f}")

Suitability range: 0.000 – 0.849



# Geographic axes from the affine transform
lon_coords = np.array([transform_ref.c + (j + 0.5) * transform_ref.a for j in range(width)])
lat_coords = np.array([transform_ref.f + (i + 0.5) * transform_ref.e for i in range(height)])

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(
    z=suit_grid,
    x=lon_coords, y=lat_coords,
    colorscale='YlGn',
    zmin=0, zmax=1,

))

title: Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling
text:
Interpretation notes
The predicted suitability map should be read with the following caveats in mind:

Background sampling matters. The partition function is approximated by the background set. If background points do not cover the full environmental space of the study region, the model will be miscalibrated in underrepresented areas.
Suitability is not probability of occurrence. The model predicts relative environmental suitability, not detectability-adjusted occupancy probability. High suitability in a pixel does not mean the species is present — it means the environment is consistent with observed presences.
Extrapolation beyond training conditions. In pixels whose environmental values fall outside the range of training data (background + presences), the network extrapolates. MaxEnt’s entropy constraint makes this extrapolation conservative by default, but it is not guaranteed to be ecologically meaningful.
Multi-species extension. The tutorial models all plant species jointly. The DeepMaxEnt loss is summed across species, allowing the shared neural backbone to learn transferable environmental features while species-specific heads capture idiosyncratic niches.
